paras: The attempted lynching of Alex Murray and Charles Shelby took place at the Livingston County jail in Chillicothe, Missouri, about 1 a.m. on the night of June 11-12, 1882, when a crowd of men demanded two young Black prisoners accused of shooting a telegraph operator. Sheriff Leeper refused to give them up and threatened to shoot, and the crowd scattered after shots were fired, with no one hurt.

Early on Sunday, June 11, two men entered the Hannibal and St. Joseph depot telegraph office and shot Fred Tucker, an assistant operator, in the cheek and thumb. A Chillicothe dispatch called it an attempt to rob the ticket office by 'a party of negroes' and said 100 or more men, including city and county officials, were in pursuit. According to the local Crisis, the men were Alex Murray and Charles Shelby, and Tucker's wounds were not dangerous.

George Graham and Policeman Tom Anderson caught Shelby that afternoon in Linn county near Meadville, and after Tucker identified him he reached the jail less than a minute ahead of a large and excited crowd. Murray was found asleep in an empty house near his mother's home about supper time and was hurried to the jail, the Crisis wrote, because searchers were known to have taken two ropes there. The Sedalia Bazoo reported open threats of lynching once the captures were known and a strong guard placed at the jail.

The Crisis said about 100 men called at the jail about 1 o'clock Sunday night and demanded Murray and Shelby. Leeper opened a downstairs window, reasoned with the men, and told them he would kill the first one who tried to enter the door. A street lamp was then shot out and someone near the sheriff fired a pistol into the air, and most of the crowd fled, believing Leeper had fired. The rest soon dispersed, and the night passed quietly.

No arrest of anyone in the crowd appears in the coverage; by the next morning, the Bazoo wrote, the danger of a lynching was considered past. The Crisis also tied the two men to the theft of four horses the same weekend, and another Black man, Hampton Arnold, was jailed on suspicion. No report of a trial was found, but in October the Crisis described Murray as 'the colored desperado, who escaped from the penitentiary,' after deputies watching for him shot another man by mistake.

Coverage came from Missouri white papers over about two weeks. The Crisis ran the fullest account under headlines calling the men two 'NEGROES, WITH MURDER AND ROBBERY IN THEIR HEARTS,' saying they were jailed 'JUST IN TIME TO SAVE THEIR NECKS,' and praising 'OUR BRAVE SHERIFF' for upholding 'THE SUPREMACY OF THE LAW.' The same story listed both men's earlier acquittals and called them guilty regardless.

The Sedalia Bazoo headlined 'THE BLACK BRUTES' and called the shooting 'as foul a murder as was ever conceived,' while reporting the jail attack under 'ATTEMPT TO LYNCH.' The Richmond Democrat and the Kirksville Graphic gave short paragraphs, the Richmond item closing 'No lynching that night.'

Accounts of the crowd differ: the Crisis gave about 100 men, the Graphic 75 masked men, and the Bazoo about thirty unmasked men. Only the Bazoo said the men crept up to surprise the guard and made 'one or two desperate assaults' on the jail before quietly dispersing. The Richmond Democrat described the prisoners as 'under arrest for stealing,' while the other papers tied their arrest to the shooting of Tucker.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Alex Murray and Charles Shelby
bases: A crowd went to the Livingston County jail at night to take and hang two jailed Black men accused of shooting a telegraph operator and was turned away by the sheriff (A2, A3, A4, A5).

No one was killed: the crowd of 30 to 100 men that demanded the prisoners to hang them dispersed after the sheriff threatened to shoot, so this was an attempted lynching, not a completed one (A2, A3, A4, A5).

The local Crisis (A2), the Richmond Democrat (A3), the Sedalia Bazoo (A4) and the Kirksville Graphic (A5) all report a crowd at the jail that sought the prisoners and was repulsed, though they differ on its size and conduct.

accounts.label: Local paper (Crisis)
accounts.gist: About 100 men called at the jail about 1 a.m. and demanded the prisoners; the sheriff reasoned with them and said he would kill the first man to enter; after a lamp was shot out and a pistol fired in the air, most fled thinking Leeper had fired.

accounts.label: Sedalia Bazoo
accounts.gist: About thirty unmasked men crept toward the jail hoping to surprise the guard, were kept at bay despite 'one or two desperate assaults,' and quietly dispersed.

accounts.label: State news paragraphs
accounts.gist: A mob determined to hang the prisoners (Richmond) or 75 masked men (Kirksville) demanded them; the sheriff threatened to shoot and a pistol shot scattered them.

framing.detail: The Crisis headlined 'CRIME RAMPANT' and the men 'WITH MURDER AND ROBBERY IN THEIR HEARTS,' said they were jailed 'JUST IN TIME TO SAVE THEIR NECKS,' and praised the sheriff for maintaining 'THE SUPREMACY OF THE LAW,' while detailing both men's past charges.
The Bazoo headlined 'THE BLACK BRUTES' and called the shooting 'as foul a murder as was ever conceived,' then reported the 'ATTEMPT TO LYNCH' and the 'lynching picnic' threat as past.
The Butler Times wire ('MORE DEVILTRY') blamed 'a party of negroes' whose 'depredations' were becoming too frequent to be endured; it predates the jail incident.
The Richmond Democrat and Kirksville Graphic gave short, flat paragraphs ending 'No lynching that night.'
